alt: The diff table of a compressed grid, headed by the original x and y coordinates. Each rectangle changes only its four corner entries, by plus 1, minus 1, minus 1 and plus 1. Then a running sum taken one row at a time turns the marks into the number of rectangles that cover each cell.

steps.caption: The diff table has one row per y value and one column per x value, all zeros: 6 by 6 for 3 rectangles. The headings are the original coordinates; the position of a heading is its rank.

Rectangle A has its corners at ranks (column 0, row 0) and (column 3, row 2). Four entries change: +1 at its top-left, -1 at its top-right, -1 at its bottom-left and +1 at its bottom-right. No other entry is touched.

Rectangle B has its corners at ranks (column 2, row 1) and (column 5, row 4). Four entries change: +1 at its top-left, -1 at its top-right, -1 at its bottom-left and +1 at its bottom-right. No other entry is touched.

Rectangle C has its corners at ranks (column 1, row 3) and (column 4, row 5). Four entries change: +1 at its top-left, -1 at its top-right, -1 at its bottom-left and +1 at its bottom-right. No other entry is touched.

All 3 rectangles are recorded with 12 small updates. The last row and column only ever hold -1 and +1 marks, so the cells are the 5 by 5 block above and to the left. A running sum over that block, one row at a time, turns marks into depths.
Row 0 (y = 0). There is no row above, so each cell adds only the cell to its left. It now reads [1, 1, 1, 0, 0].
Row 1 (y = 20). Each cell adds the cell above and the cell to its left, then subtracts the cell above and to the left, which was added twice. It now reads [1, 1, 2, 1, 1].
Row 2 (y = 30). Each cell follows the same rule as in row 1. It now reads [0, 0, 1, 1, 1].
Row 3 (y = 60). Each cell follows the same rule as in row 1. It now reads [0, 1, 2, 2, 1].
Row 4 (y = 80). Each cell follows the same rule as in row 1. It now reads [0, 1, 1, 1, 0].
Every cell now holds how many rectangles cover it. A cell holding 0 is uncovered; the areas come from multiplying by each cell's width and height, which the next figure does.
